source_text: Quod vero ais: Quia concupiscentia qui licite commiscetur, malo bene utitur [n230] , ut magis credi Apostolo commemores, qui dixisset quia non habitat in carne sua bonum, et hoc non bonum, id est malum in carne Apostoli habitans, vis concupiscentiam carnis videri [n231] , Manichaeus non aliter quam tu posuit. Nam postquam dixit: Ne manifestentur opera eorum; propter quod Apostolus - inquit - clamat ad Romanos: " Non bonum quod volo ago, sed malum operor quod exhorreo " [n232] . Dolebat enim - inquit - quia peccatum id est diabolus operabatur in eo omnem concupiscentiam, legalis auctoritas indicat malum concupiscentiae, cum omnem eius usum vituperat, quem caro miratur et laudat.
pass_a_gloss: But what you say: Because who is licitly mixed by desire uses an evil well, that you commemorate the Apostle more to be believed, who had said that good does not dwell in his flesh, and this not-good, that is evil dwelling in the flesh of the Apostle, you want to seem the desire of the flesh, the Manichaean has placed not otherwise than you. For after he said: Lest their works be manifested; on account of which the Apostle, he says, cries to the Romans: Not the good which I will I do, but I work the evil which I abhor. For he was grieving, he says, because sin, that is the devil, was working in him every desire; legal authority indicates the evil of desire, when it vituperates every use of it, which the flesh admires and praises.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: You say: ‘Anyone who has lawful intercourse through desire uses an evil well’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36). You remind us to believe instead the apostle, who said good did not dwell in his flesh, and you want what is not good—that is, the evil dwelling in the apostle’s flesh—to be understood as fleshly desire (Romans 7:18). Mani put it no differently. After saying, ‘So that their deeds will not be exposed,’ he adds: ‘This is why the apostle cries to the Romans: “I do not do the good I want, but I perform the evil I abhor” (Romans 7:19) (John 3:20). He grieved because sin—that is, the devil—produced every desire in him (Romans 7:8). The law’s authority shows desire’s evil by condemning every use of it, which the flesh admires and praises.’

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
